note: Clipped from 'buenos días / buenas tardes', so it works at any hour. Very common in Spain when walking into a shop or bar: informal but perfectly polite.
One of a family of 'hasta' farewells: 'hasta luego', 'hasta mañana', 'hasta la vista' (until the seeing), 'hasta ahora' (back in a moment).
Greetings use the plural. Used from lunch (2-3 pm in Spain) until it gets dark. 'Tarde' as an adverb also means 'late'.
Both a greeting after dark and a farewell at bedtime. 'Noche' is from Latin 'nox, noctis' (cf. 'nocturnal').
Spain's all-purpose 'OK', from 'valer' (to be worth); heard dozens of times a day. '¿Vale?' = OK? Latin America says 'bueno', 'dale' (Argentina) or 'órale' (Mexico).

example.target: Nos vemos a las ocho, ¿vale? — Vale.
example.en: See you at eight, OK? — OK.

note: The most common everyday farewell in Spain. 'Hasta' (until) came into Spanish from Arabic 'ḥattā'.
'Mañana' means both 'tomorrow' and 'morning' ('por la mañana' = in the morning). The ñ sounds like the 'ny' of 'canyon', a word English took from Spanish 'cañón'.
Reflexive 'nos' + 'vemos' (from 'ver', to see). Casual, very common among friends in Spain and Latin America.
The standard reply to 'mucho gusto', 'buen provecho' or 'que tengas un buen día'. From 'igual' (equal, same), Latin 'aequalis'.
Plural of 'felicidad'. Used for birthdays, weddings and good news. Spain also says 'enhorabuena' (literally 'in good hour') for achievements.
Short for 'no hay de qué' (there is nothing to thank for). Latin America also uses 'con gusto' (with pleasure).
Cognate of English 'pardon'. For small things: bumping into someone, getting attention, asking to repeat. For real apologies use 'lo siento' (I feel it).
The 'usted' command form of 'oír' (to hear); 'oye' is the informal version. The normal way to call a waiter or stop a stranger, and not rude at all in Spanish.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

note: The 'usted' command form of 'disculpar', built on 'culpa' (blame, cf. English 'culprit'). To a friend: 'disculpa'. Used to start a question to a stranger.
Informal all-purpose greeting. Also asks for an opinion: '¿Qué tal la película?' (How was the film?). Every Spanish question opens with an inverted ¿.
Uses 'estar', the verb for temporary states, not 'ser'. The formal version drops the -s: '¿Cómo está (usted)?'

example.en: Hi, how are you? — Very well, and you?

note: Short for 'mucho gusto en conocerle'. Typical replies: 'igualmente' (likewise) or 'el gusto es mío' (the pleasure is mine).
Agrees with the speaker: a woman says 'encantada'. Cognate of English 'enchanted'; the full form is 'encantado de conocerte'.
'Bien' (well) + 'venido' (past participle of 'venir', to come). Agrees with the person: 'bienvenida', plural 'bienvenidos'.
Said when clinking glasses and when someone sneezes (like German 'Gesundheit'). From Latin 'salus', the root of 'salute' and 'salutary'.
'Provecho' means profit or benefit. In Spain it is normal to say it to strangers eating nearby; 'que aproveche' is a common variant.
Said when squeezing past someone, leaving a table or entering a room. Especially frequent in Latin America.
From Latin 'senior' (older). 'Señora' = Mrs/madam; 'señorita' (Miss) is now used less for adult women. Lower-case unless abbreviated: Sr., Sra.
A contraction of 'vuestra merced' (your grace), which is why it takes he/she verb forms. Abbreviated Ud. In Latin America the plural 'ustedes' replaces 'vosotros' entirely.

literal: that you may have a good day
note: A wish introduced by 'que' takes the subjunctive ('tengas', from 'tener'). The formal version is 'que tenga un buen día'.
From Arabic 'ṣifr' via medieval Latin 'zephirum'; English 'zero' and 'cipher' come from the same word. Pronounced 'thero' in Spain, 'sero' in Latin America.
Shortens to 'un' before a masculine noun ('un libro') and becomes 'una' before a feminine one ('una casa'). 'Uno' stands alone when counting.
From Latin 'duos'. Invariable: 'dos chicos', 'dos chicas'. 'Los dos' = both.
From Latin 'tres', same root as English 'three'. Rhymes with 'dos' and 'seis'; 'los tres' = all three.
From Latin 'quattuor'. The Latin 'qu' became Spanish 'cu' before a vowel; compare 'cuánto' (how much).
From Latin 'quinque'. 'Cinco de Mayo' is a Mexican holiday; 'las cinco' = five o'clock.
From Latin 'sex'. Pronounced like English 'say-ss'. Combined forms: 'dieciséis' (16), 'veintiséis' (26).
From Latin 'septem'; the Latin 'e' broke into 'ie', a very common Spanish change (cf. 'tierra' from 'terra').
From Latin 'octo'; the Latin 'ct' regularly became Spanish 'ch' ('noche' from 'noctem'). English keeps the 'ct' in 'octave'.
From Latin 'novem'. The same 'o' > 'ue' change gives 'nuevo' (new). 90 is 'noventa'.
From Latin 'decem' (cf. 'decimal'). The final z is pronounced 'th' in Spain and 's' in Latin America. 'Diez' is the base of 'dieci-' in 16-19.
From Latin 'undecim'. 11 to 15 are single words ending in -ce: once, doce, trece, catorce, quince.
From Latin 'duodecim'. 'Las doce' = twelve o'clock; 'una docena' = a dozen.
From Latin 'tredecim'. In Spain the unlucky day is Tuesday the 13th ('martes y trece'), not Friday.
From Latin 'quattuordecim'. Pronounced ca-TOR-ce, stress on the middle syllable.
From Latin 'quindecim'. 'Quince días' (fifteen days) is the usual way to say 'two weeks'. A girl's 15th birthday ('la quinceañera') is a big celebration in Latin America.
'Diez y seis' fused into one word; the written accent keeps the stress on 'séis'. 17-19 follow the pattern: diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve.
From Latin 'viginti'. 21-29 are one word: 'veintiuno', 'veintidós'. From 31 up they are written with 'y': 'treinta y uno'.
From Latin 'triginta'. The other tens end in -enta: cuarenta (40), cincuenta (50), sesenta (60), setenta (70), ochenta (80), noventa (90).
Short form of 'ciento', used before a noun ('cien euros') and for exactly 100. 'Ciento' returns in 101+ ('ciento dos'); 200 is 'doscientos' (feminine 'doscientas').
Never 'un mil': 1000 is just 'mil', 2000 'dos mil'. From Latin 'mille' (cf. 'millennium', 'mile' = a thousand paces).
Drops the -o before a masculine singular noun: 'el primer día'. Then segundo, tercero (tercer), cuarto, quinto, sexto, séptimo, octavo, noveno, décimo.

example.en: I live on the first floor.

note: Also the noun 'a second' of time. Ordinals above 10 are rarely used in speech: people say 'el piso quince', not 'el decimoquinto'.
'Medio kilo', 'media hora' (half an hour), 'las dos y media' (half past two). As a noun 'la mitad' is 'the half' of something.
'Un par de días' = a couple of days; loosely 'a few', like English. Also literally a pair: 'un par de zapatos'.
Latin 'familia'. Spanish and Latin American family life often includes the extended family; 'la familia política' = the in-laws.
Latin 'mater'. Children say 'mamá' (stress on the last syllable). 'Madre mía' is a common exclamation of surprise.
Latin 'pater'. 'Papá' is the affectionate form. 'Padre' is also a priest ('Father').
The masculine plural covers a mixed group, so 'los padres' = parents and 'los hijos' = children (sons and daughters). Context decides whether it means 'fathers'.
From Latin 'filius'. Latin initial f- regularly became a silent Spanish h-: 'harina' (flour, farina), 'hacer' (facere), 'hierro' (ferrum).
From Latin 'germanus' (of the same parents); silent h. 'Los hermanos' = siblings. 'Hermano' is also a friendly address like 'bro'.
From Latin 'aviolus', diminutive of 'avus'. 'Los abuelos' = grandparents. Affectionate forms: 'abuelito', 'yayo' (Spain).
From Latin 'nepos'. 'Los nietos' = grandchildren. English 'nephew' and 'nepotism' share the root.
From Greek 'theios' via Late Latin. In Spain 'tío/tía' is also very common slang for 'guy' / 'girl' ('¡Oye, tío!').
From Latin 'consobrinus primus' (first cousin); the 'first' is all that survived. 'Primo' is also slang for someone easily fooled.
From Latin 'maritus'. 'Esposo' is the more formal word; 'esposa' is the usual word for wife.
From Latin 'mulier'. Means both 'woman' and 'wife' ('mi mujer' = my wife). The j is a throaty h-sound.
From Latin 'hominem'. The -mbr- cluster is typical Spanish: 'nombre' (name), 'hambre' (hunger). '¡Hombre!' is also an exclamation ('Come on!', 'Well!').
'El Niño', the Pacific climate pattern, is named after the Christ Child because it appears around Christmas. 'Los niños' = children.
For teenagers and young adults; 'chico' is also an adjective meaning 'small'. Latin America also says 'muchacho/muchacha'.
From Latin 'cognatus' (related by blood). 'Los suegros' are the parents-in-law. In recent Spanish slang a 'cuñado' is also the know-it-all who holds forth at family dinners.
Stress on the final syllable. Masculine regardless of sex in Spain; parts of Latin America use 'la bebé' for a girl or say 'la beba'.
Grammatically singular: 'la gente es amable' (people are kind). From Latin 'gens, gentis' (cf. 'gentle', 'gentile').

example.target: Hay mucha gente en la calle.
example.en: There are a lot of people in the street.

note: Always feminine, even for a man: 'Juan es una persona seria'. From Latin 'persona', originally an actor's mask.
Covers boyfriend/girlfriend as well as fiancé and bride/groom ('los novios' = the couple at a wedding). From Latin 'novius' (new).
From Latin 'vicinus' (cf. 'vicinity'). Also 'resident': 'los vecinos de Madrid' = the people of Madrid.
From Latin 'sobrinus' (cousin on the mother's side); the meaning shifted. 'Los sobrinos' = nephews and nieces.
Both 'a couple' and 'partner' of either sex: 'mi pareja' avoids stating marital status. From 'par' (pair).
Spaniards and Latin Americans have two surnames: the father's first, then the mother's. Women keep their own surnames after marriage.
From Latin 'vota' (vows). 'Las bodas de oro' = golden wedding anniversary. 'Casarse' is 'to get married'.
From Latin 'panis' (cf. 'pantry', 'companion' = someone you share bread with). 'Una barra de pan' is a baguette-style loaf in Spain.
Feminine, but takes 'el' in the singular because it starts with a stressed a-: 'el agua fría', 'las aguas'. Order 'agua con gas' or 'sin gas' (sparkling/still).

example.target: Un vaso de agua, por favor.

note: From Latin 'lac, lactis' (cf. 'lactose'). The Latin 'ct' became Spanish 'ch'. 'Café con leche' is the standard breakfast coffee.
From Latin 'caseus', the same source as English 'cheese' and German 'Käse'. 'Queso manchego' is the best-known Spanish cheese.
From Latin 'ovum'; words beginning with the 'ue' sound get a written h-. 'Huevos fritos' = fried eggs; 'tortilla' in Spain is an egg and potato omelette.
From Latin 'caro, carnis' (cf. 'carnivore', 'carnival'). Also 'flesh'. 'Carne de res' = beef in Latin America ('ternera' in Spain).
From Latin 'pullus' (young animal, cf. 'pullet'). The ll is pronounced like y. Not to be confused with 'polo' (polo shirt / ice lolly).
Past participle of 'pescar' (to fish). The live animal is 'el pez'; once caught and on a plate it becomes 'pescado'.

example.target: Prefiero el pescado a la carne.

note: From Arabic 'ar-ruzz'; rice cultivation came to Spain with the Moors, and Valencia is the home of paella. Final z = 'th' in Spain.
From Arabic 'az-zayt' (olive oil); the 'a-' is the fused Arabic article, as in 'azúcar', 'almohada', 'alcalde'. Spain is the world's largest producer of olive oil.
'Fruta' is fruit you eat; 'el fruto' is the botanical or figurative fruit ('el fruto del trabajo'). Both from Latin 'fructus'.
From Latin 'mala mattiana', a variety named after a Roman farmer, Matius. 'Manzana' is also a city block in Spanish.
From Arabic 'nāranj', ultimately Persian and Sanskrit; English 'orange' came the same way via French. The colour is 'naranja' too.

example.target: Un zumo de naranja, por favor.

note: The word in Spain; Latin America mostly says 'banana' or 'banano', and uses 'plátano' for the cooking plantain.
From 'verde' (green). Usually plural: 'las verduras'. 'Legumbres' are pulses, 'hortalizas' is the broader word for garden produce.
Spain only; the rest of the Spanish-speaking world says 'la papa', the original Quechua word from the Andes, where the potato comes from. 'Patatas bravas' is a classic tapa.
From Nahuatl 'tomatl' (Aztec), like 'chocolate' and 'aguacate'. English 'tomato' came through Spanish.
From Arabic 'as-sukkar'; the English word came through Old French. Gender wavers: 'azúcar moreno' or 'morena' (brown sugar) are both heard.
From Latin 'sal' (cf. 'salary', 'salad'). Feminine. 'Salado' = salty; 'sin sal' = unsalted.
From Latin 'vinum'. 'Vino tinto' is red wine (not 'rojo'); 'vino blanco' white; 'rosado' rosé. Rioja and Ribera del Duero are the big Spanish regions.

example.target: Una copa de vino tinto, por favor.
example.en: A glass of red wine, please.

note: From Latin 'cervesia', a Gaulish word. In Spain a small draught beer is 'una caña'; Latin America often says 'una chela' (Mexico) or 'una birra'.
Stress on the final é. 'Café solo' = espresso; 'cortado' = with a splash of milk; 'café con leche' = half milk. Also means the café itself.
Cured 'jamón serrano' and acorn-fed 'jamón ibérico' are Spain's signature foods. Cooked ham is 'jamón de York' in Spain. The j is a throaty h.
Regular -er verb. Also 'to have lunch' in Spain ('la comida' = the midday meal). The -éis ending of 'coméis' is the 'vosotros' form used in Spain only.

example.en: What do you want to eat?

note: Regular -er verb, from Latin 'bibere' (cf. 'beverage', 'imbibe'). Latin America often prefers 'tomar' (to take) for drinking.
From French 'restaurant'. Spanish lunch is around 2-3 pm and dinner rarely before 9 pm; many kitchens close in between.
A Spanish 'bar' is a daytime café as much as a pub: coffee, breakfast, tapas and beer. Spain has one of the highest numbers of bars per person in the world.
Spain. Latin America says 'mesero/mesera' (from 'mesa', table) or 'mozo' (Argentina). Call them with 'perdone' or 'por favor', not by snapping.
The full menu is 'la carta'; 'el menú (del día)' is the fixed-price set lunch of starter, main, dessert and drink, a Spanish institution.

example.en: Could you bring me the menu, please?

note: From 'contar' (to count). Also 'account' (bank account = 'cuenta bancaria'). In Spain the bill is not brought until you ask for it.
From Latin 'mensa'. English 'mesa' (a flat-topped hill) was borrowed from Spanish. 'Una mesa para dos' = a table for two.
Tipping is modest in Spain (rounding up or a euro or two); 10% is more expected in Mexico and much of Latin America.
'Des-' (un-) + 'ayuno' (fast), exactly like English 'break-fast'. A Spanish breakfast is small: coffee and a 'tostada' or pastry.
From Latin 'admordium' (a bite); the al- is not Arabic here. In Spain the main midday meal is usually just 'la comida'; 'almuerzo' is standard in Latin America.
From Latin 'cena' (dinner). 'Cenar' = to have dinner. 'La Última Cena' is the Last Supper. Spaniards eat it late, 9-10 pm.
Said to come from the slice of ham or bread laid over a glass as a 'lid'. 'Ir de tapas' = to go bar-hopping for small plates. Free with a drink in Granada and León.
From 'bocado' (mouthful), from 'boca' (mouth). A Spanish 'bocadillo' is on a baguette; 'un sándwich' is on sliced bread. Latin America says 'torta' (Mexico) or 'sándwich'.
Germanic origin, shared with English 'soup' and 'sop'. 'Gazpacho' is the cold Andalusian tomato soup.
From 'sal' (salt), like English 'salad' from Latin. 'Ensalada mixta' (lettuce, tomato, tuna, egg) is on almost every Spanish menu.
From Latin 'post' (after): what comes after the meal. 'De postre' = for dessert. 'Flan' and 'arroz con leche' are the classics.
A tumbler (water, beer). A stemmed wine glass is 'una copa'. English 'vase' is a cognate but the meaning differs: a false friend.
From Arabic 'ṭassa' (bowl). 'Una taza de café' = a cup of coffee. Also the toilet bowl in colloquial use.
From French 'bouteille', from Late Latin 'butticula'. 'Una botella de agua' = a bottle of water; 'el botellón' is an outdoor street drinking gathering in Spain.
From 'tener' (to hold). The noun suffix -dor names a tool or doer, like English -er ('ordenador', 'jugador').
From Latin 'cultellus', diminutive of 'culter' (ploughshare, knife). The ll is a y-sound: cu-CHI-yo.
From Latin 'cochlearium' (snail-shell spoon). 'Cucharilla' or 'cucharita' is a teaspoon. Note it is feminine, unlike 'cuchillo'.
Stem-changing e > i in all forms except 'we' and 'you (pl.)'. 'Pedir' = ask for something; 'preguntar' = ask a question.

example.en: What are you going to order?

note: Regular, but the g becomes gu before e to keep the hard sound: 'pagué' (I paid). From Latin 'pacare', to appease, hence 'pay'.
Stem-changing o > ue. Means 'taste' for food, 'try on' for clothes ('probarse') and 'prove' in formal use. Cognate of English 'prove'.
Spanish 'has' hunger, thirst, heat and years: 'tengo sed' (thirsty), 'tengo calor' (hot), 'tengo 20 años'. 'Hambre' is feminine but takes 'el' ('el hambre').
From Latin 'viaticum' (provisions for the road), the same source as English 'voyage'. '¡Buen viaje!' = have a good trip.
Regular -ar verb. 'Viajar en tren / en avión' (by train / plane), 'viajar por España' (around Spain).
From French 'passeport': a document to pass through a 'port' or city gate. 'El DNI' is the Spanish national ID card used for travel within the EU.
Silent h. 'Un hostal' is a cheaper guesthouse; 'un parador' is a state-run hotel in a historic building, a Spanish speciality.
From Latin 'habitare' (to dwell). 'Habitación doble / individual' = double / single room. Latin America often says 'cuarto' or, in Mexico, 'recámara' for a bedroom.

example.en: Do you have a room free?

note: From Late Latin 'plagia'; French 'plage' is the same word. 'Ir a la playa' = go to the beach; 'playero' = beach (adj.).
Masculine despite ending in -a, from medieval Latin 'mappa mundi' (cloth of the world). Other -ma/-pa masculines: 'el problema', 'el idioma', 'el clima'.
From Latin 'callis' (path). Abbreviated 'C/' on addresses: 'C/ Mayor, 5'. 'Calle' also appears in the Caribbean music hit 'Calle 13'.
'A la derecha' = on / to the right. 'Derecho' (masc.) means 'straight ahead' and also 'law' and 'a right'. The political right is also 'la derecha'.

example.target: La farmacia está a la derecha.
example.en: The pharmacy is on the right.

note: Borrowed from Basque 'ezkerra', one of very few Basque words in everyday Spanish; it pushed out the Latin 'sinistra'. 'A la izquierda' = on the left.
'Siga todo recto' = keep going straight. Latin America more often says 'derecho' or 'siga derecho'. 'Recto' is from Latin 'rectus' (cf. 'rectangle').
An outside corner, where two streets meet: 'en la esquina'. An inside corner of a room is 'el rincón'. 'Hacer esquina' = to be on the corner.
From Latin 'circa' (around). Takes 'de' before a noun: 'cerca de la estación'. 'Cercano' is the adjective ('nearby').
'Lejos de' = far from. 'Lejano' is the adjective: 'el Lejano Oeste' (the Far West). 'A lo lejos' = in the distance.
Latin America commonly uses 'acá' with the same meaning. 'Aquí mismo' = right here; 'por aquí' = around here / this way.
Spanish has three distances: 'aquí' (here), 'ahí' (there, near you), 'allí' (over there). 'Allá' is the vaguer 'over there', more used in Latin America.
'Estar' is used for location, never 'ser'. In Spain you will also hear 'los servicios' or 'el aseo'; 'el baño' is the word everywhere in Latin America.
From 'salir' (to go out). On a sign: EXIT; on a timetable: departures ('salidas' / 'llegadas'). 'Salida de emergencia' = emergency exit.
From 'entrar'. Besides 'entrance' it means an admission ticket (cinema, museum, concert) and a starter course. Transport tickets are 'billetes', not 'entradas'.
From Latin 'gyrare' (cf. 'gyrate'). 'Gire a la derecha' = turn right. Latin America often says 'doblar' or 'voltear' instead.

example.target: Gira a la izquierda en el semáforo.
example.en: Turn left at the traffic lights.

note: From Latin 'plicare' (to fold the sails); Latin 'pl-' became Spanish 'll-' ('lluvia' from 'pluvia'). 'Llegar tarde' = to be late; 'llegar a' = arrive at.

example.target: El tren llega a las diez.

note: Irregular 'yo' form 'salgo'. From Latin 'salire' (to jump). 'Salir con alguien' = to go out with / date someone; 'salir bien' = turn out well.
Reflexive form of 'perder' (to lose), stem-changing e > ie. 'Me he perdido' = I'm lost. Also 'to miss' an event: 'no te lo pierdas' (don't miss it).
'Hacer la maleta' = to pack. 'Maletero' is the car boot/trunk. Argentina and Uruguay say 'valija'; 'equipaje' is luggage in general.
Same form for both sexes; only the article changes, as with all '-ista' nouns ('el/la artista', 'el/la dentista'). Spain is one of the world's most visited countries.
Spain. Latin America says 'el carro' (Mexico, Caribbean, Andes) or 'el auto' (Argentina, Chile). 'Coche' comes from Hungarian 'kocsi', after the town of Kocs, like English 'coach'.
Stress on the final syllable. Regional words vary wildly: 'camión' (Mexico), 'guagua' (Cuba, Canary Islands), 'colectivo' (Argentina), 'micro' (Chile).
From French 'train'. Spain's high-speed network, the AVE ('Alta Velocidad Española'), is one of the longest in the world; 'ave' also means 'bird'.
From Latin 'avis' (bird); the French pioneer Clément Ader coined 'avion'. Plural 'aviones'. 'En avión' = by plane.
'Aero' + 'puerto' (port, harbour). Stress: ae-ro-PUER-to. Madrid-Barajas and Barcelona-El Prat are Spain's busiest.
Also 'season' of the year ('las cuatro estaciones'). Latin 'st-' gets an e- in Spanish: 'estación', 'estudiante', 'España'. 'Estación de tren / de metro / de autobuses'.
Short for 'ferrocarril metropolitano'. Madrid's opened in 1919; Buenos Aires's 'subte' (1913) was the first in Latin America. 'Metro' is also the unit of length.
Plural 'taxis'. 'Coger un taxi' (take a taxi) is normal in Spain, but 'coger' is vulgar in Mexico and Argentina, where people say 'tomar un taxi'.
Shortened to 'la bici' in speech. 'Ir en bici' = to cycle. 'La Vuelta a España' is the Spanish equivalent of the Tour de France.
From Latin 'barca'; English 'embark' and 'barque' share the root. A small boat is 'una barca'; 'el ferry' is used for car ferries.
Spain's word for both a transport ticket and a banknote. Latin America uses 'boleto' for tickets and keeps 'billete' for banknotes.

example.target: Un billete para Sevilla, por favor.

note: From 'volar' (to fly). 'Vuelo directo' = direct flight; 'vuelo de ida y vuelta' = return flight. Iberia is the Spanish flag carrier.
From 'parar' (to stop). 'Parada de autobús', 'parada de taxis' (taxi rank). 'Próxima parada' is the announcement you hear on board.
Plural 'andenes'. '¿De qué andén sale?' = which platform does it leave from? Also used for a station's platform in Latin America; 'vía' (track) is given on Spanish departure boards.
'Ida' is from 'ir' (to go), 'vuelta' from 'volver' (to return). A single is 'solo ida'. Mexico says 'viaje redondo'.
Spain. Latin America says 'el chofer' or 'chófer', from French 'chauffeur'. A bus driver is 'el conductor del autobús'.
Irregular 'yo' form 'conduzco', shared by all -ducir verbs ('traducir', 'producir'). Latin America says 'manejar' (to handle) instead.
Regular -ir verb. 'Subir al tren' = get on the train; 'subir la escalera' = go upstairs; 'subir un archivo' = upload a file.
From 'bajo' (low). 'Bajar del autobús' = get off the bus; 'bajar' also = download, and lower (the volume, a price).

example.en: Where do I have to get off?

note: 'Gasolinera' is a petrol station. Argentina says 'nafta', Chile 'bencina'. Diesel is 'gasóleo' or 'diésel'.
From Greek 'sema' (signal) + 'phoros' (bearer). 'En el semáforo' = at the lights. 'Semáforo en rojo / en verde'.
From Latin 'camminus', a word of Celtic origin. 'El Camino de Santiago' is the pilgrimage route; 'de camino a' = on the way to.
'Pista' is a track, runway or dance floor. A toll motorway is 'autopista de peaje'; 'autovía' is the toll-free equivalent in Spain. 'Carretera' is any main road or highway.
'Ir a pie' = to walk there. Compare 'de pie' = standing, 'en pie' = still standing / valid. 'Pie' is from Latin 'pes, pedis' (cf. 'pedal').

example.target: Está a diez minutos a pie.

note: From 'atrás' (behind). 'Con retraso' = late, delayed; 'el tren lleva veinte minutos de retraso'. Latin America also says 'demora' or 'atraso'.
Silent h; from Latin 'hora'. '¿A qué hora?' = at what time? 'Es hora de comer' = it's time to eat. 'Hora punta' = rush hour.
Means both 'time' and 'weather', like French 'temps'. 'No tengo tiempo' (no time); 'hace buen tiempo' (nice weather). A specific occasion is 'una vez', not 'un tiempo'.
Masculine despite ending in -a (from Latin 'dies'). 'Todos los días' = every day; 'al día' = up to date; 'hoy en día' = nowadays.
From Latin 'septimana' (seven-day period). 'La semana que viene' = next week; 'Semana Santa' = Holy Week, a major holiday in Spain and Latin America.
From Latin 'mensis'. Plural 'meses'. 'Al mes' = per month; 'el mes pasado' = last month. Month names are written in lower case in Spanish.
From Latin 'annus'. Age uses 'tener': 'tengo treinta años'. Mind the ñ: 'ano' without the tilde means 'anus'. '¡Feliz Año Nuevo!' = Happy New Year.
From Latin 'hodie'. Silent h, rhymes with 'soy'. 'Hoy en día' = nowadays; 'de hoy' = today's.
'Mañana' = tomorrow; 'la mañana' = the morning; 'mañana por la mañana' = tomorrow morning. 'Pasado mañana' = the day after tomorrow.
From Latin 'ad heri'. 'Anteayer' or 'antes de ayer' = the day before yesterday. 'Ayer por la noche' = last night.
From Latin 'hac hora' (at this hour). 'Ahora mismo' = right now. In Mexico the diminutive 'ahorita' can mean 'right away', 'in a while' or, famously, 'never'.
From Latin 'dies Lunae'. Days are masculine and lower case. 'El lunes' = on Monday, 'los lunes' = on Mondays; Monday to Friday keep the same form in the plural.
From Latin 'dies Martis'. Tuesday the 13th ('martes y trece') is the unlucky date in the Spanish-speaking world, not Friday.
From Latin 'dies Mercurii'. Written accent on the 'é'; stress mi-ÉR-co-les. English 'Wednesday' honours the equivalent god Woden.
From Latin 'dies Iovis' (Jove). Latin America and Spain alike: 'Jueves Santo' = Maundy Thursday.
From Latin 'dies Veneris'. 'Viernes Santo' = Good Friday. 'Por fin es viernes' = TGIF.
From Hebrew 'shabbat' via Latin 'sabbatum', unlike the English 'Saturn's day'. Plural 'los sábados'.

example.target: El sábado vamos a la playa.
example.en: On Saturday we're going to the beach.

note: From Latin 'dies dominicus' (the Lord's day). Spanish-speaking calendars begin the week on Monday, so Sunday is the last column.
From Latin 'Ianuarius' (Janus). Months are lower case. The rest: febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre.
Named after Emperor Augustus. In Spain much of the country shuts down for holidays in August. 'Hacer su agosto' = to make a killing (from the harvest profits).
From Latin 'december' (the tenth month of the old Roman year, 'decem'). Christmas Eve, 'Nochebuena' (24 December), is the main family celebration.
Shortened to 'el finde' in casual Spanish from Spain. 'El fin de semana pasado' = last weekend.
Answers use 'ser': 'Es la una' (singular for one o'clock), 'Son las tres y cuarto' (quarter past three), 'Son las ocho menos diez' (ten to eight).
From Latin 'temporanus' (timely). 'Levantarse temprano' = get up early. The opposite is 'tarde' (late).
The noun covers roughly 1 pm to dark; the adverb 'tarde' means 'late': 'llego tarde' (I'm late). 'Por la tarde' = in the afternoon.
From Latin 'horologium' via Catalan 'rellotge'. One word for both clock and wristwatch ('reloj de pulsera'). The final j is barely pronounced; plural 'relojes'.
Masculine, like most nouns in -or ('el calor', 'el amor'). '¿De qué color es?' = what colour is it? 'En color' vs 'en blanco y negro'.
From Latin 'russus'. Red wine is 'tinto', never 'rojo'. 'Ponerse rojo' = to blush. The j is a throaty h: RO-ho.
From Arabic 'lāzaward' (lapis lazuli), the same root as English 'azure'. Same form for masculine and feminine; plural 'azules'. 'Azul marino' = navy blue.
From Latin 'viridis'. Also 'unripe' and, for jokes, 'dirty' ('un chiste verde'). Same form m/f; the party is 'los Verdes'.
The double l sounds like y: a-ma-RI-yo. 'Prensa amarilla' = tabloid press. The Spanish flag is 'rojo y amarillo' (or 'rojigualda').
From Latin 'niger'. 'Mercado negro' = black market; 'novela negra' = crime fiction. 'Café solo' is the usual way to order a black coffee in Spain.
Germanic origin (cf. English 'blank', French 'blanc'). 'En blanco' = blank; 'vino blanco' = white wine; 'Casablanca' = white house.
Germanic word that reached Spanish through Old Provençal. Same form m/f; plural 'grises'. 'Un día gris' = a grey, dull day.
Spain, from French 'marron' (chestnut); plural 'marrones'. For hair and eyes use 'castaño'; Latin America usually says 'café' for brown objects.
Also the flower ('una rosa'). As a colour it is usually invariable: 'zapatos rosa'. 'La prensa rosa' = celebrity gossip press; 'novela rosa' = romance novel.
Same word as the fruit; invariable as a colour ('camisetas naranja'). 'Anaranjado/a' is the formal adjective that does agree.
From 'mora' (mulberry, blackberry). 'Un morado' is also a bruise, and 'ponerse morado' means to stuff yourself with food.
'Azul claro' = light blue. From Latin 'clarus' (clear). '¡Claro!' on its own means 'of course!'; 'claro que sí' = yes, of course.
From Latin 'obscurus'. 'Azul oscuro' = dark blue; 'a oscuras' = in the dark. The older spelling 'obscuro' is still accepted but rare.
'En forma de corazón' = heart-shaped. Also 'way': 'de esta forma' = in this way; and fitness: 'estar en forma' = to be fit.
From Latin 'circulus'. Written accent on the first syllable. Also a social circle; 'círculo vicioso' = vicious circle.
From 'cuatro' (four). A town square is 'la plaza', never 'cuadrado'. As an adjective: 'metros cuadrados' = square metres.
'Tri-' (three) + 'ángulo' (angle). The accent marks the stress: tri-ÁN-gu-lo. Also the percussion instrument.
From Latin 'linea' (linen thread). 'En línea' = online; 'línea 2 del metro' = metro line 2; 'mantener la línea' = keep one's figure.
Also 'full stop' in punctuation and 'point' in a score. 'A las dos en punto' = at two o'clock sharp; 'punto com' = dot-com.

example.target: Nos vemos a las ocho en punto.

note: From Latin 'rotundus'. 'Una mesa redonda' = a round table (also a panel discussion). 'Un número redondo' = a round number.
From Latin 'stella'. Latin words beginning with 's' + consonant gain an 'e' in Spanish: 'estrella', 'escuela', 'España'. Also a celebrity ('estrella de cine').
'A rayas' = striped. Also a parting in the hair and the dash in writing. 'Pasarse de la raya' = to cross the line, go too far.
From 'luna' (moon). 'Un vestido de lunares' is the classic polka-dot flamenco dress. The same word is a beauty spot or mole on the skin.
From Latin 'crux'. Plural 'cruces'. 'Cara o cruz' = heads or tails (coins show a 'face' and a 'cross'). 'La Cruz Roja' = the Red Cross.
From Latin 'corpus' (cf. 'corpse', 'corporal'). 'Cuerpo' is also a corps: 'el cuerpo de bomberos' = the fire brigade.
From Latin 'caput' via 'capitia'. 'Dolor de cabeza' = headache; 'cabeza de ajo' = a head of garlic. The z is 'th' in Spain, 's' in Latin America.
Also the 'heads' side of a coin and 'nerve': 'tener mucha cara' = to be cheeky. 'Cara a cara' = face to face. Latin America also uses 'el rostro'.
From Latin 'oculus'; the 'cul' became the throaty 'j'. '¡Ojo!' = watch out! 'Ojalá' (hopefully) is unrelated: it is Arabic 'in shāʾ Allāh'.
Plural 'narices'. 'Estar hasta las narices' = to be fed up to the back teeth. The pig's snout is 'el hocico'.
From Latin 'bucca' (cheek). 'Boca abajo / boca arriba' = face down / face up. Argentina's famous football club is Boca Juniors, after the port district.
From Latin 'dens, dentis' (cf. 'dentist'). Plural 'dientes'. A molar is 'una muela'; 'dolor de muelas' = toothache. 'Diente de ajo' = a clove of garlic.
The visible ear. The inner ear and the sense of hearing are 'el oído': 'dolor de oído' = earache. From Latin 'auricula'.
Feminine despite ending in -o, because Latin 'manus' was feminine: 'la mano derecha', 'las manos'. 'Echar una mano' = to lend a hand.
From Latin 'brachium'. 'Un abrazo' (a hug) is built on it and is the standard warm sign-off in emails and messages.
From Latin 'perna' (ham, leg of pork). Animals and furniture have 'patas', not 'piernas'. 'Estirar las piernas' = stretch one's legs.
From Latin 'pes, pedis'. Plural 'pies'. 'A pie' = on foot; 'de pie' = standing; 'al pie de la letra' = to the letter.
From Late Latin 'spatula' (shoulder blade), the same word as the kitchen 'spatula'. 'Dolor de espalda' = backache. The back of an object is 'la parte de atrás'.
Stress on the 'tó'. 'Dolor de estómago' = stomach ache. Colloquially 'la barriga' or 'la tripa' (Spain) = belly, tummy.
From Latin 'cor' plus the augmentative '-ón'. Plural 'corazones'. 'De todo corazón' = with all my heart; 'mi corazón' is a term of endearment.
From Latin 'sanguis'. Feminine. The drink 'sangría' is named after its blood-red colour. 'Análisis de sangre' = blood test.
'Doctor/a' is used as a title when addressing one. 'La médica' is now standard for a woman, though 'la médico' is still heard. 'Ir al médico' = to go to the doctor.
Silent h, stress on the last syllable: os-pi-TAL. Plural 'hospitales'. 'Urgencias' is A&E / the emergency room.
Marked by a green cross in Spain. 'Farmacia de guardia' = the duty pharmacy open at night. Latin America also says 'droguería' (Colombia) or 'botica'.
'Dolor de cabeza / de garganta / de espalda' = headache / sore throat / backache. The name Dolores comes from 'la Virgen de los Dolores' (Our Lady of Sorrows).
Works like 'gustar': the body part is the subject and the person is an object pronoun. 'Me duele la cabeza' (my head hurts), 'me duelen los pies' (plural). Stem o > ue.
Stem-changing o > ue. 'Dormir la siesta' = to have a nap; 'siesta' (from Latin 'sexta hora', the sixth hour, midday) is one of English's best-known Spanish loans.
Use with 'estar': 'estoy enfermo' (I'm ill). From Latin 'infirmus' (weak). 'Enfermero/a' = nurse; 'enfermedad' = illness.
From Latin 'febris'. 'Tener fiebre' = to have a temperature. Figuratively any craze: 'la fiebre del oro' = the gold rush.
A classic false friend: 'estar constipado' means to have a cold, not to be constipated (that is 'estreñido'). 'Un resfriado' is the cold itself.
From Latin 'casa' (hut). 'En casa' = at home, 'a casa' = (to) home, no article. 'Casa' also means a company or a brand ('la casa Seat').
In Spain 'piso' is a flat; it also means 'floor, storey' ('tercer piso'). Latin America says 'apartamento' or 'departamento' (Mexico, Argentina) and uses 'piso' only for the floor.
From Latin 'porta'. Madrid's central square is the 'Puerta del Sol' (Gate of the Sun), once a city gate. 'Puerto' (port, harbour) is the sibling word.
Built on 'viento' (wind): the opening where the wind comes in. A shop window is 'el escaparate' (Spain) or 'la vitrina'.
Means both the room and the stove ('cocina de gas'). 'Cocinero/a' = cook, chef. 'La cocina española' = Spanish cuisine.
From 'dormir' (to sleep). Also 'la habitación' or 'el cuarto'; in Mexico 'la recámara'. Note it is not a 'dormitory' in the student-hall sense ('residencia').
Augmentative of 'sala' (hall). Spain says 'salón' or 'sala de estar'; Latin America says 'la sala' or, in Argentina, 'el living'. English 'saloon' and 'salon' are cousins.
'Ir a la cama' = go to bed; 'hacer la cama' = make the bed; 'cama de matrimonio' = double bed. 'Guardar cama' = to stay in bed when ill.
From Latin 'sella' (seat). 'Sillón' = armchair; 'silla de ruedas' = wheelchair. The ll is a y-sound: SI-ya.
Masculine, stress on the final -á, plural 'sofás'. From Arabic 'ṣuffa' (bench) via French. 'Sofá cama' = sofa bed.
From Latin 'clavis'; Latin 'cl-' became Spanish 'll-' ('llamar' from 'clamare'). Also a tap in Latin America (Spain: 'grifo') and a spanner ('llave inglesa', English key).
From Latin 'lux'. Plural 'luces'. 'La luz' is also the electricity bill ('pagar la luz'). 'Dar a luz' = to give birth.
From Latin 'solum' (cf. 'soil', 'sole'). In Spain 'suelo' is the floor you stand on; Latin America says 'el piso'. 'Suelo' is also farmland soil.
A wall of a building, inside or out. A freestanding or garden wall is 'el muro'; a city wall is 'la muralla'. Plural 'paredes'.
From French 'douche', from Italian 'doccia'. 'Ducharse' = to have a shower; 'darse una ducha'. A bath is 'la bañera' / 'bañarse'.
From French 'jardin', a Germanic word related to 'garden' and 'yard'. Plural 'jardines'. 'Jardín de infancia' = kindergarten; a vegetable plot is 'la huerta'.
From 'nieve' (snow): originally a snow pit or icebox. Spain's word; elsewhere 'el refrigerador', 'el refri' (Mexico), 'la heladera' (Argentina).
From 'lavar' (to wash) + the tool suffix '-dora'. 'Poner la lavadora' = put a wash on. 'Lavavajillas' = dishwasher; 'lavaplatos' in Latin America.
From Latin 'speculum' (cf. 'speculate', originally to observe). 'Mirarse al espejo' = look at oneself in the mirror. Spanish 'mirar' has nothing to do with it.
From Arabic 'al-mukhadda', from 'khadd' (cheek): the thing for the cheek. 'Consultarlo con la almohada' = to sleep on it. One of hundreds of Arabic 'al-' words in Spanish.

example.target: Lo voy a consultar con la almohada.
example.en: I'm going to sleep on it.

note: From 'escala' (Latin 'scala', ladder). One word for stairs and ladder; 'escalera mecánica' = escalator. Often plural 'las escaleras' for a staircase.
Borrowed into English from Spanish. In Spain it is the inner courtyard of a house, famous in Córdoba; 'patio de recreo' = school playground; 'patio de butacas' = theatre stalls.
Regular -ir verb from Latin 'vivere'. Both 'reside' and 'be alive'. '¡Viva España!' is its subjunctive ('long live').
Regular -ar verb from 'cocina'. 'Cocer' is the narrower 'to boil/stew'. '¿Quién cocina hoy?' = who's cooking today?
From 'limpio' (clean), Latin 'limpidus' (cf. 'limpid'). 'Limpiar la casa' = clean the house; 'limpieza' = cleaning, cleanliness.
A singular collective noun: 'la ropa está limpia' (the clothes are clean). From Gothic, related to English 'robe'. 'Ropa interior' = underwear.
From Late Latin 'camisia', the source of 'chemise'. 'Camisón' = nightdress. 'En mangas de camisa' = in shirtsleeves.
Diminutive of 'camisa'. Also a football shirt. Regional words: 'playera' (Mexico), 'remera' (Argentina), 'polera' (Chile), 'franela' (Venezuela).
Usually plural for one pair: 'los pantalones'. From French 'pantalon', after Pantalone, the Venetian character of the commedia dell'arte who wore them.
Past participle of 'vestir' (to dress) used as a noun. 'Vestido de novia' = wedding dress. Masculine, although it is worn by women.
Germanic origin (related to 'fold'). Also the lower slope of a mountain ('la falda de la montaña'). Argentina and parts of the Andes say 'pollera'.
From French 'jaquette'. Latin America has many words: 'saco' (suit jacket), 'chamarra' (Mexico), 'campera' (Argentina). Avoid 'chaqueta' in Mexico, where it is vulgar slang.
From 'abrigar' (to shelter, keep warm). 'Al abrigo de' = sheltered from. 'Ropa de abrigo' = warm clothes.
Spain, from the island of Jersey; plural 'jerséis'. Latin America says 'suéter' (from English) or 'pulóver'; the Andes say 'chompa'.
Plural 'zapatos'. 'Zapatería' = shoe shop; 'zapatero' = shoemaker, also 'Zapatero, a tus zapatos' = stick to what you know.
Spain, often 'zapatillas de deporte'; also house slippers ('zapatillas de casa'). Latin America mostly says 'tenis'.
From 'calza' (hose), Latin 'calceus' (shoe). Plural 'calcetines'. In Latin America socks are usually 'medias', which in Spain means stockings.
A woolly winter scarf. A silk scarf or headscarf is 'un pañuelo', which also means handkerchief and tissue.
From 'sombra' (shade). English borrowed it for the wide Mexican hat, but in Spanish it is any brimmed hat. A woolly hat is 'un gorro'.
A peaked cap (baseball cap). 'El gorro' is a brimless woolly or swimming hat. 'De gorra' = free, scrounging ('entrar de gorra').
Always plural, Spain's word. Latin America says 'lentes' (Mexico, Andes) or 'anteojos' (Argentina). 'Gafas de sol' = sunglasses.
Spain. 'La bolsa' is a shopping or plastic bag; 'el bolsillo' is a pocket. In Latin America a handbag is usually 'la cartera' or 'la bolsa' (Mexico).
Augmentative of 'cintura' (waist). 'Cinturón de seguridad' = seat belt; 'apretarse el cinturón' = tighten one's belt. Plural 'cinturones'.
'¿Qué talla tiene?' = what size are you? Shoe size is 'el número', and the size of an object is 'el tamaño'. 'Talla única' = one size.

en: to wear; to carry; to take
note: Regular. 'Llevar un vestido' = wear a dress; 'llevar a alguien' = take someone somewhere; 'llevo dos años aquí' = I've been here two years. 'Para llevar' = takeaway.

example.en: He is wearing a blue shirt.

note: Reflexive of 'poner' (to put); irregular 'pongo'. Also 'to become': 'ponerse rojo' (blush), 'ponerse nervioso'. 'Ponerse el sol' = to set (the sun).
Reflexive of 'quitar' (to remove). 'Quítate los zapatos' = take off your shoes. 'Quitarse de en medio' = get out of the way.
Stem-changing e > i, like 'pedir'. From Latin 'vestire' (cf. 'vest', 'invest'). 'Vestirse de negro' = dress in black; 'vestirse de' = dress up as.
From 'traer' (to bring). 'Traje de baño' = swimsuit (Spain also 'bañador'); 'traje de luces' is the bullfighter's 'suit of lights'; 'traje de novia' = wedding dress.
From 'vaca' (cow): 'pantalones vaqueros' = cowboy trousers, Spain's word for jeans. Latin America says 'jeans' or, in Mexico, 'pantalones de mezclilla'.
From Vulgar Latin 'tripaliare', to torture on a 'tripalium' (three-stake rack); French 'travail' has the same grim origin. 'Buscar trabajo' = look for a job.
Regular -ar verb. 'Trabajar de camarero' = to work as a waiter; 'trabajar en' = work at/in. The j is a throaty h.

example.en: What do you do for a living?

note: From Latin 'officina' (workshop). 'Oficina de turismo' = tourist office. A private office or study is 'el despacho'.
Also 'enterprise, undertaking'. 'Empresario/a' = businessman/woman, entrepreneur; 'pequeña y mediana empresa (pyme)' = SME.
From French 'chef' (chief). A Spanish 'jefe' is any boss; a kitchen chef is 'el chef' or 'el cocinero jefe'. 'Jefe de estudios' = head of studies at a school.
Literally a 'bread-sharer' ('con' + 'pan'), exactly like English 'companion'. 'Compañero de clase / de trabajo / de piso' = classmate / colleague / flatmate.
From 'reunir' (to gather). Any work meeting, not only a 'reunion' of old friends, a partial false friend. 'Estar en una reunión' = to be in a meeting.
From Latin 'solidus', a Roman gold coin that also gave English 'soldier' (a paid man) and 'solid'. 'Salario' is the more formal synonym.
From Latin 'schola'; Spanish adds an 'e' before 's' + consonant. Mostly primary school; 'el colegio' is the usual word for school in Spain, 'el instituto' for secondary.
Shortened to 'la uni'. Salamanca (1218) is Spain's oldest. 'Universitario/a' = university student or adjective. Plural 'universidades'.
Same form for both sexes; 'la estudianta' is non-standard. School pupils are 'alumnos'. 'Estudiante de Medicina' = medical student.
Any teacher from secondary school up, shortened to 'profe'. Primary teachers are 'maestros' (Spain) or 'maestros/profesores' (Latin America).

example.target: La profesora de español es de Colombia.
example.en: The Spanish teacher is from Colombia.

note: The lesson, the group and the classroom ('en clase'). Also 'kind': 'toda clase de' = all kinds of. 'Tener clase' = to have class / to be classy.
Plural 'exámenes' gains an accent to keep the stress. 'Aprobar' = to pass; 'suspender' = to fail (a false friend, not 'suspend').
From Latin 'liber' (originally tree bark). Watch the false friend: 'librería' is a bookshop; a library is 'la biblioteca'.

example.target: Estoy leyendo un libro muy bueno.
example.en: I'm reading a very good book.

note: Spain's word, from 'deber' (to have to; a duty). Latin America says 'la tarea'. 'Hacer los deberes' = do one's homework.
Spain's word, from French 'ordinateur'. Latin America says 'la computadora' or 'el computador'. 'Portátil' = laptop.
'El correo' = the post; 'Correos' is Spain's postal service. In speech people say 'un correo', 'un mail' or 'un email'. 'Enviar un correo' = send an email.
Regular. 'Estudiar Derecho / Medicina' = to study law / medicine (no article). 'El estudio' = the study, a studio, or a studio flat.
From Latin 'apprehendere' (to grasp), the root of 'apprentice'. Takes 'a' before an infinitive: 'aprender a nadar' (learn to swim).
From Latin 'insignare' (to mark, cf. 'sign'). Both 'teach' and 'show': 'enséñame la foto' = show me the photo. 'Enseñanza' = teaching, education.
From Latin 'legere'. Regular in the present, but the past has 'leyó / leyeron' and the gerund is 'leyendo' (i between vowels becomes y).
From Latin 'scribere' (cf. 'scribe'). Regular except for the past participle 'escrito' (written). 'Escritor/a' = writer.
Masculine despite the -a (a Greek '-ma' word, like 'el problema'). It means a language, not an 'idiom' (that is 'un modismo'). 'La lengua' is both tongue and language.
'Hacer una carrera' = to do a university degree; 'carrera profesional' = career; 'carrera de coches' = car race. From 'carro' (cart): originally a cart road.
From Latin 'sol'. 'Hace sol' = it's sunny; 'tomar el sol' = to sunbathe. Also Peru's currency and the musical note. 'Solo' (alone) is unrelated.
From Latin 'pluvia'; Latin 'pl-' became Spanish 'll-'. 'Un día de lluvia' = a rainy day; 'lluvioso' = rainy.
Impersonal: only the 'it' forms exist. Stem-changing o > ue ('llueve'). 'Llueve a cántaros' (it rains by the pitcherful) = it's raining cats and dogs.
From Latin 'nix, nivis'. 'Nevada' (the US state) means 'snow-covered', as in Spain's Sierra Nevada. 'Copo de nieve' = snowflake.
Impersonal, stem-changing e > ie: 'nieva' (it snows) but 'nevó' (it snowed). 'Nevada' = a snowfall.
From Latin 'ventus'. 'Hace viento' = it's windy. 'Ventana' (window) and 'ventilador' (fan) are built on it.
From Latin 'nubes'. 'Nublado' = cloudy, overcast. 'Estar en las nubes' = to have one's head in the clouds; 'la nube' = the (computing) cloud.
From Latin 'caelum' (cf. 'celestial'). One word for sky and heaven. 'Mi cielo' is a term of endearment, like 'sweetheart'.
'Hace frío' (the weather is cold), 'tengo frío' (I am cold), 'está frío' (the soup is cold). Never 'estoy frío' for feeling cold. From Latin 'frigidus'.
Masculine in standard Spanish ('el calor'), though 'la calor' is heard in Andalusia. 'Hace calor' = it's hot; 'tengo calor' = I'm hot. From Latin 'calor' (cf. 'calorie').
Weather is described with 'hacer' (to make/do): 'hace calor, frío, sol, viento, mal tiempo'. 'Bueno' shortens to 'buen' before a masculine noun.
From Latin 'tormentum', the same source as 'torment'. 'Tormenta de nieve' = blizzard. Figurative too: 'una tormenta de ideas' = brainstorming.
Masculine in everyday use ('el mar Mediterráneo') but feminine among sailors and poets ('la mar'). From Latin 'mare' (cf. 'marine'). 'La mar de' = loads of.
From Latin 'rivus' (stream), which also gave 'rival' (people sharing a stream). The accent separates 'río' from 'rio' (he laughed). Río de la Plata, Río Grande.
From Latin 'montanea', from 'mons'. The US state Montana is the Spanish adjective 'mountainous'. 'La sierra' (saw) is a jagged range.
Germanic origin, related to English 'bush' and French 'bois'. A jungle or rainforest is 'la selva'. 'El Bosque de Chapultepec' is Mexico City's great park.
From Latin 'arbor' (feminine in Latin, masculine in Spanish). Written accent on the á; plural 'árboles'. 'Árbol genealógico' = family tree.
From Latin 'flos, floris'. Feminine. Florida was named 'Pascua Florida' (flowery Easter) by Ponce de León. Plural 'flores'.
From Latin 'campus' (cf. 'camp', 'campus', 'champion'). 'Ir al campo' = go to the countryside; 'campo de fútbol' = football pitch.
From Latin 'insula' (cf. 'insular', 'peninsula' = almost-island). Silent-looking 's' is fully pronounced: IS-la. 'Las Islas Canarias', 'las Baleares'.
From Latin 'focus' (hearth), which English took in the optical sense. '¿Tienes fuego?' = have you got a light? 'Fuegos artificiales' = fireworks.
From Latin 'terra'. Lower-case 'tierra' = soil, ground, land; capital 'la Tierra' = the planet. 'Tierra del Fuego' = Land of Fire. 'Mi tierra' = my homeland.
Spelled exactly like English, from Latin 'animal' (a breathing thing, from 'anima'). Plural 'animales'. Stress on the last syllable: a-ni-MAL.
Of unknown origin; it replaced Latin 'canis', which survives in 'canino'. Roll the double r. 'Perrito caliente' = hot dog. 'Perra' can be an insult, like English.
From Late Latin 'cattus'. Also a car jack. 'Hay gato encerrado' (there's a cat shut in) = something fishy is going on. 'Gatito' = kitten.
From Latin 'tendere' (to stretch): originally an awning or tent, and 'tienda de campaña' still means tent. 'Tienda de ropa' = clothes shop.
From Latin 'mercatus' (cf. 'merchant'). Every Spanish town has a covered food market, the 'mercado de abastos'. 'Mercadillo' = street market, flea market.
Shortened to 'el súper' in speech. 'Ir al súper' = go to the supermarket. Mercadona and Carrefour are the big chains in Spain.
From Latin 'denarius', a Roman silver coin. Slang: 'pasta' (Spain), 'plata' (silver, Latin America), 'lana' (wool, Mexico). 'Dinero en efectivo' = cash.
From Latin 'pretium' (cf. 'price', 'precious', 'appreciate'). '¿Qué precio tiene?' = what's the price? 'A mitad de precio' = half price.
From Latin 'carus' (dear). Unlike English 'dear', it only means costly; 'querido' is 'dear' as in beloved. 'Salir caro' = to prove costly.
'¡Qué barato!' = how cheap! The adverb is also 'barato': 'comer barato' = to eat cheaply. 'Baratija' = a trinket, cheap thing.
'Tarjeta de crédito / de débito' = credit / debit card; also a business card, a greetings card and a boarding pass ('tarjeta de embarque'). '¿Con tarjeta o en efectivo?'
'En efectivo' = in cash. As an adjective it means 'effective'. 'Sacar dinero' = to withdraw cash; a cash machine is 'un cajero (automático)'.
Masculine, plural 'euros'. Spain adopted it in 2002, replacing the peseta. Cents are 'céntimos'. Prices are written with a comma: 3,50 €.
'Quédese con el cambio' = keep the change. Also exchange rate and bureau de change ('casa de cambio'). 'En cambio' = on the other hand.
From 'rebajar' (to lower). 'Las rebajas de enero' are Spain's big January sales. An individual offer is 'una oferta'; a discount 'un descuento'.
'Regalar' = to give as a present. 'De regalo' = as a free gift. The verb also means 'to give away cheaply': 'lo están regalando' = they're practically giving it away.
A shopping or plastic bag, and the stock exchange ('la Bolsa'). From Latin 'bursa' (cf. 'purse', 'bursar'). 'Bolsa de basura' = bin bag.
'Ir al centro comercial' = go to the mall. Mexico also says 'la plaza' for a mall; the historic 'centro' of a city is a different thing.
From Latin 'comparare' (to procure). 'Ir de compras' = to go shopping; 'hacer la compra' = do the food shopping. 'Comprador' = buyer.
From Latin 'vendere' (cf. 'vendor'). 'Se vende' on a sign = for sale. 'Vendedor/a' = seller, shop assistant.
Stem-changing o > ue; used mostly in the 'it/they' forms. Also 'to be hard for': 'me cuesta levantarme' = I find it hard to get up.
Spend money (time is 'pasar'), and wear out or use up ('gastar las pilas'). Related to English 'waste'. 'Los gastos' = expenses; 'gastar una broma' = play a joke.
Alternatives: '¿Cuánto es?' (how much is it, when paying) and '¿Cuánto vale?'. For several items: '¿Cuánto cuestan?'

example.en: How much does this shirt cost?

note: Irregular past participle of 'abrir' (to open). Use with 'estar': 'la tienda está abierta'. 'Abierto' on a door sign; also 'open-minded' for people.
From 'cerrar' (to close; 'cierro', e > ie). 'Cerrado por vacaciones' is a common August sign in Spain. Also 'closed-minded', and a thick accent ('acento cerrado').
From Latin 'capsa' (cf. 'case', 'capsule'). The till ('pagar en caja'), a box, and a bank ('caja de ahorros'). 'Cajero automático' = ATM.
From 'carta' (letter): originally a letter case. Spain: wallet, briefcase, portfolio; Latin America: handbag. 'Cartero/a' = postman/woman.
Pure Latin, invariable: 'la entrada es gratis'. 'Free' as in freedom is 'libre', a distinction English blurs. The adjective is 'gratuito/a'.
From Latin 'felix'. Same form for m/f; plural 'felices'. 'Feliz cumpleaños', 'Feliz Navidad'. 'Ser feliz' = to be a happy person; 'estar feliz' = to be happy right now.
From Latin 'tristis'. Same form m/f. Used with 'estar': 'estoy triste'. 'La tristeza' = sadness. Also 'dreary': 'un día triste'.
Always with 'estar' (a mood, not a trait): 'estoy muy contenta'. 'Contento con' = happy with. From Latin 'contentus' (satisfied).

example.target: Estoy muy contento con el resultado.
example.en: I'm very pleased with the result.

note: 'Estar cansado' = to be tired; 'ser cansado' = to be tiring, tiresome. A neat ser/estar contrast. 'Cansarse de' = to get tired of.
Spain's word; Latin America says 'enojado/a'. With 'estar': 'está enfadada conmigo' (she is angry with me). 'Enfadarse' = to get angry.
Nervous, jittery, on edge, used with 'estar'. 'Ponerse nervioso' = to get nervous. 'Los nervios' = nerves, also 'stage fright'.
From Latin 'tranquillus'. '¡Tranquilo!' on its own = relax, take it easy. 'Un barrio tranquilo' = a quiet neighbourhood.
The textbook ser/estar pair: 'estoy aburrido' = I'm bored; 'soy aburrido' = I'm boring. 'Aburrirse' = to get bored. From Latin 'abhorrere'.
Literally 'pre-occupied'. 'Estar preocupado por' = to be worried about. 'No te preocupes' = don't worry (one of the most useful Spanish phrases).
From Latin 'amor'. 'Mi amor' = my love (endearment, also to children). 'Amor propio' = self-respect. 'Hacer el amor' = make love.
From Latin 'metus'. Fear is 'had': 'tengo miedo' = I'm afraid, 'tener miedo de' = to be afraid of. 'Dar miedo' = to be scary; 'una película de miedo' = a horror film.
From 'alegre' (cheerful), Latin 'alacer' (cf. 'alacrity'). '¡Qué alegría!' = how lovely! 'Alegrías' is also a lively flamenco style from Cádiz.
Stem-changing e > ie. 'Quiero un café' (I want) and 'te quiero' (I love you). From Latin 'quaerere' (to seek), the root of 'query' and 'question'.

example.en: Do you want to come with us?

note: Back-to-front: the thing liked is the subject. 'Me gusta el café' = coffee pleases me; plural 'me gustan los gatos'. From Latin 'gustare' (to taste; cf. 'gusto'). Say 'me gustas' only to flirt.
Literally 'to enchant', built like 'gustar': 'me encanta Madrid', 'me encantan los libros'. Stronger than 'gustar' and never needs 'mucho'.
From 'odio' (hatred), Latin 'odium'. Regular -ar verb. '¡Lo odio!' = I hate it. 'Odiar' is strong; 'no soporto' (I can't stand) is milder.
From Latin 'plorare' (cf. 'deplore', 'implore'); Latin 'pl-' became 'll-'. 'Llorón/llorona' = crybaby; 'La Llorona' is a famous Mexican ghost legend and song.
Often reflexive: 'reírse de' = to laugh at. The accents mark a stressed í in every form. From Latin 'ridere' (cf. 'ridiculous'). 'La risa' = laughter.
The everyday 'I love you' for partners, family and close friends. 'Te amo' is more intense and romantic, and more common in Latin America than in Spain.

en: to feel like / look forward to
note: 'Tengo ganas de verte' = I'm looking forward to seeing you; 'no tengo ganas' = I don't feel like it. 'Con ganas' = with gusto. 'Gana' alone is rare; 'ganar' = to win, earn.
From Arabic 'in shāʾ Allāh' (God willing), the most famous Arabic loan in Spanish. It is followed by the subjunctive: 'ojalá llueva' (I hope it rains), 'ojalá pudiera' (if only I could).

The dots on the ü show that the u is pronounced ('ver-GWEN-tha'). 'Tener vergüenza' = to be embarrassed or shy; '¡qué vergüenza!' = how embarrassing. 'Vergüenza ajena' = cringe on someone else's behalf.
Built on 'amor'. 'Estar enamorado de' = to be in love with; 'enamorarse' = to fall in love. 'El Día de los Enamorados' = Valentine's Day.
Past participle of 'sorprender', from French 'surprendre'. 'La sorpresa' = surprise; '¡qué sorpresa!' = what a surprise.
From Latin 'sors, sortis' (lot, fate; cf. 'sort'). '¡Suerte!' or '¡Buena suerte!' = good luck; 'tener suerte' = to be lucky; 'por suerte' = luckily.
Stem-changing e > ie. 'Pensar en' = think about; 'pienso que' = I think that; 'pensar + infinitive' = to plan to. From Latin 'pensare' (to weigh; cf. 'pensive').
For where something is and how it is right now: 'estoy en casa', 'está cansado', 'estamos bien'. From Latin 'stare' (to stand; cf. 'state', 'status'). Also forms the progressive: 'estoy comiendo'.

example.en: Where are you? — I'm on the train.

note: Irregular 'tengo', stem e > ie. From Latin 'tenere' (to hold; cf. 'tenant'). 'Tener que' = to have to. Also age and sensations: 'tengo 30 años', 'tengo sed'.
From Latin 'facere' (Latin f- became silent h-). Irregular 'hago', participle 'hecho'. Used for weather ('hace frío') and 'ago': 'hace dos años' = two years ago.

example.en: What are you doing this weekend?

note: Spanish's most irregular verb, patched together from Latin 'ire', 'vadere' ('voy') and 'esse' ('fui'). 'Ir a + infinitive' = going to (future). '¡Vamos!' = let's go.
Irregular 'vengo', stem e > ie, like 'tener'. From Latin 'venire' (cf. 'advent', 'convene'). 'La semana que viene' = next week; 'venir de' = come from.
Stem-changing o > ue. '¿Puedo?' = may I? 'No puedo más' = I can't go on. The noun 'el poder' = power. From Latin 'potere' (cf. 'potent', 'possible').
Irregular 'digo', stem e > i, participle 'dicho'. From Latin 'dicere' (cf. 'dictate'). '¿Cómo se dice...?' = how do you say...?; 'es decir' = that is to say.

example.en: How do you say 'thanks' in Spanish?

note: From Latin 'videre' (cf. 'video', 'view'). Participle 'visto'. 'A ver' = let's see; 'ver la tele' = watch TV; 'nos vemos' = see you.
From Latin 'dare', which also gave 'data' (things given). Irregular 'doy' like 'voy', 'soy', 'estoy'. 'Dar un paseo' = take a walk; 'dar a' = to overlook ('la ventana da al mar').
Knowing facts and skills: 'sé nadar' = I can swim; 'no sé' = I don't know. Also 'to taste': 'sabe a ajo' (it tastes of garlic). From Latin 'sapere' (cf. 'savour', 'sapient'). Note the accent on 'sé'.
Being familiar with people, places and things: 'conozco Madrid'. 'Conocer a alguien' = to meet someone for the first time. Irregular 'conozco'; from Latin 'cognoscere' (cf. 'recognise').
From Latin 'fabulari' (to tell tales, cf. 'fable'), with f- > h-. The model regular -ar verb. '¿Habla inglés?' = do you speak English? 'Hablar de' = talk about.
Reflexive of 'levantar' (to lift, raise). 'Me levanto a las siete' = I get up at seven. 'Levantarse de la mesa' = to leave the table.
Spanish has single verbs for the meals: 'desayunar', 'comer/almorzar', 'cenar'. Regular -ar; '¿Qué desayunas?' = what do you have for breakfast?
Stem o > ue, participle 'vuelto'. 'Volver a + infinitive' = to do again: 'vuelvo a empezar' = I start again. From Latin 'volvere' (cf. 'revolve'). 'Volver' is also a famous Almodóvar film.
Stem e > ie; the z becomes c before e in the past ('empecé'). 'Empezar a + infinitive' = to start doing. 'Comenzar' is the more formal synonym.
Regular -ar, from Latin 'terminus' (boundary). 'Terminar de + infinitive' = to finish doing. 'Acabar' is the everyday synonym; 'acabo de llegar' = I've just arrived.

en: to wait; to hope; to expect
note: One verb for all three: 'espero el autobús' (wait for), 'espero que sí' (hope so, with subjunctive), 'esperamos un bebé' (expecting). 'Sala de espera' = waiting room.
No preposition: 'busco mi llave' (I'm looking for my key). The c becomes qu before e: 'busqué'. 'Buscador' = search engine; 'buscar en Google' = to google.
Regular -ar from Latin 'necessitas'. 'Necesito ayuda' = I need help. Spelling trap: one c, one s, like the noun 'necesidad'.
From Latin 'clamare' (cf. 'clamour'), with cl- > ll-. Reflexive 'llamarse' = to be called: '¿Cómo te llamas?' (how do you call yourself?) 'Me llamo Ana'. 'Llamar por teléfono' = to phone.
The only u > ue stem-changing verb. 'Jugar al fútbol' (Spain adds 'al'; Latin America often just 'jugar fútbol'). Playing an instrument is 'tocar', not 'jugar'.
Regular -ir verb except for the participle 'abierto'. From Latin 'aperire' (cf. 'aperture'). '¿A qué hora abren?' = what time do they open?
'Tomar el metro', 'tomar una decisión', 'tomar el sol' (sunbathe). In Latin America it is also the normal word for 'to drink'. The safe choice where 'coger' is vulgar (Mexico, Argentina).
The accent marks a question or exclamation: '¿Qué es esto?', '¡Qué bonito!'. Without it, 'que' means 'that/which'. '¿Qué tal?' = how's it going?
Plural 'quiénes' when asking about several people. '¿De quién es?' = whose is it? '¿Con quién?' = with whom? From Latin 'quem'.
'¿Dónde está?' = where is it? '¿Adónde vas?' = where are you going (to)? '¿De dónde eres?' = where are you from? No accent in 'el pueblo donde vivo'.
Accent only in questions: '¿Cuándo llegas?'. Unaccented 'cuando' = when as a conjunction ('cuando llueve'). '¿Desde cuándo?' = since when?
'¿Cómo estás?', '¿Cómo te llamas?'. A bare '¿Cómo?' = pardon? Without accent 'como' means 'like, as' and also 'I eat'.
Agrees with the noun: 'cuánta gente', 'cuántos años', 'cuántas veces'. '¿Cuánto es?' = how much is it? '¡Cuánto tiempo!' = long time no see.

example.en: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

note: Two words with an accent when asking. 'Porque' (one word, no accent) = because, and 'el porqué' = the reason. '¿Por qué no?' = why not?
One word, no accent, as opposed to the question 'por qué'. '¿Por qué estudias español? — Porque me gusta.' 'Por' alone = for/because of: 'por eso' = that's why.
Use before 'es' and when choosing: '¿Cuál es tu nombre?' (not 'qué'), '¿Cuál prefieres?'. Plural 'cuáles'. 'Qué' goes directly before a noun: '¿Qué libro?'
With the accent. Without it, 'si' = if. 'Sí' also stresses a verb: 'sí quiero' = I do want to. 'Sí mismo' = oneself; 'creo que sí' = I think so.
Both 'no' and 'not', placed before the verb: 'no sé' = I don't know. Double negatives are correct Spanish: 'no veo nada' = I don't see anything.
Becomes 'e' before a word starting with i- or hi-: 'padres e hijos'. Likewise 'o' (or) becomes 'u' before o-: 'siete u ocho'. 'Y' is pronounced like 'ee'.
After a negative, 'but rather' is 'sino': 'no es rojo, sino azul'. 'Pero' is the general 'but'. Do not confuse with 'perro' (dog): one r, not rolled.
From 'tan bien' (so well). 'Yo también' = me too. The negative counterpart is 'tampoco' (neither): 'yo tampoco' = me neither.
Before adjectives and adverbs: 'muy bien', 'muy grande'. Never before a verb or alone: use 'mucho' there ('me gusta mucho'). 'Muy' + comparative is wrong: 'mucho mejor', not 'muy mejor'.
As an adjective it agrees: 'mucha gente', 'muchos libros', 'muchas gracias'. As an adverb after a verb it is fixed: 'trabaja mucho'. From Latin 'multus'.

example.en: There are a lot of people.

note: 'Un poco de' = a bit of ('un poco de agua'); 'poca gente' = few people; 'poco a poco' = little by little. From Latin 'paucus' (cf. 'paucity').
From Latin '(res) nata' (a born thing, i.e. anything at all), which turned negative. 'No quiero nada' (double negative is standard). 'De nada' = you're welcome; 'nada más' = nothing else.
From Latin 'aliquod'. '¿Algo más?' = anything else? (shop question). Also 'somewhat': 'algo cansado' = a bit tired. 'Alguien' = someone.
From Latin 'semper' (cf. 'sempiternal'). 'Para siempre' = forever; 'como siempre' = as usual; 'siempre que' = whenever / provided that.
From Latin 'nunquam'. Either before the verb ('nunca voy') or after with 'no' ('no voy nunca'); both are correct. 'Nunca jamás' = never ever. 'Jamás' is the stronger synonym.
From Latin 'cum'. Two fused forms survive: 'conmigo' (with me) and 'contigo' (with you). 'Con permiso', 'café con leche'.
From Latin 'sine'. 'Sin azúcar' = without sugar; 'sin gas' = still (water). 'Sin embargo' = however. The adjective 'sin techo' = homeless.
Purpose, destination, deadline, recipient: 'para ti', 'para mañana', 'para aprender'. Cause and exchange use 'por': 'gracias por', 'por la mañana'. 'Para llevar' = to take away.

example.target: Es un regalo para mi madre.
example.en: It's a present for my mother.

note: The accent separates it from 'tu' (your). 'Tutear' = to address someone as 'tú'. In Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America 'vos' replaces it, with its own verb forms ('vos tenés').
Same form m/f. Shortens to 'gran' before a singular noun, where it tends to mean 'great': 'una gran ciudad'. After the noun it means 'big': 'una ciudad grande'. From Latin 'grandis'.
'Pequeñito' is the affectionate diminutive. Latin America often prefers 'chico/a' or 'chiquito/a'. The comparative is the irregular 'menor' or 'más pequeño'.
Shortens to 'buen' before a masculine singular noun: 'un buen día'. 'Ser bueno' = good (quality, character); 'estar bueno' = tasty, or colloquially 'hot' for a person.
Shortens to 'mal' before a masculine singular noun: 'un mal día'. 'Ser malo' = bad; 'estar malo' = to be ill (Spain) or gone off (food). 'Mal' is also the adverb 'badly'.
From Latin 'novus'. Position matters: 'un coche nuevo' = brand new; 'un nuevo coche' = a new (different) car. Nueva York, Nuevo México.
From Latin 'vetulus'. For people and worn things; 'antiguo' for old buildings and antiques. 'Mi viejo / mi vieja' = my old man / mum, affectionate in Latin America.
Same form m/f; plural 'jóvenes' gains an accent. As a noun, 'los jóvenes' = young people, 'un joven' = a young man. From Latin 'iuvenis' (cf. 'juvenile').
For people, places and things: 'una casa bonita'. Also the fish (bonito tuna, an English loan). Latin America often says 'lindo/a'.
From Latin 'foedus'. Also 'nasty' of situations: 'una situación fea'. 'Está feo que...' = it's not nice that...
Spain's everyday word for attractive, also used as a friendly address ('¡hola, guapa!'). In Argentina 'guapo' traditionally means brave or tough; much of Latin America prefers 'lindo' for looks.
From Latin 'altus' (cf. 'altitude'). Tall people, high mountains and loud voices ('en voz alta'). '¡Alto!' = stop! (from German 'halt'). 'Alta velocidad' = high speed.
Short in height (people), low (prices, voices). 'Planta baja' = ground floor. Also the preposition 'under' and the bass guitar ('el bajo').
Same form m/f, from Latin 'fortis' (cf. 'fortitude'). Also loud, intense, heavy: 'un café fuerte', 'un fuerte abrazo' (the usual warm sign-off in messages).
Same form m/f; plural 'fáciles'. From Latin 'facilis' (doable, from 'facere'). 'Es fácil de entender' = it's easy to understand. The adverb is 'fácilmente'.
Same form m/f; plural 'difíciles'. Accent on the second í. 'Es difícil de decir' = it's hard to say. 'Complicado' is the everyday synonym.
From Latin 'rapidus'. Also the adverb 'quickly': '¡Rápido!' = hurry up! The formal adverb is 'rápidamente'; 'deprisa' is a common synonym in Spain.
A false friend: it means likeable, friendly, not 'sympathetic' (that is 'comprensivo'). 'Me cae simpático' = I find him likeable. 'Antipático' = unfriendly.
Same form m/f. For objects and food: 'agua caliente', 'perrito caliente'. For people 'estar caliente' means sexually aroused, so say 'tengo calor' (I'm hot).
From Latin 'limpidus'. With 'estar': 'la casa está limpia'. 'Jugar limpio' = to play fair; 'pasar a limpio' = to write out a fair copy.
From Latin 'sucidus'. 'Ropa sucia' = dirty laundry; 'jugar sucio' = to play dirty; 'dinero sucio' = dirty money. The c is 'th' in Spain.
From Latin 'plenus' (cf. 'plenty'), with pl- > ll-. 'Estoy lleno' = I'm full (after eating); 'lleno de gente' = full of people; 'lleno' at a petrol station = fill it up.
From Latin 'vacivus' (cf. 'vacant', 'vacuum'). Accent on the í. 'El vacío' as a noun = the void, a vacuum. 'Vaciar' = to empty.
The famous ser/estar pair: 'ser listo' = to be clever; 'estar listo' = to be ready. '¿Estás lista?' = are you ready? '¡Listo!' = done!
Rich in money ('una familia rica') and, for food, delicious: '¡qué rico!'. Puerto Rico = rich port; Costa Rica = rich coast. Germanic origin, related to English 'rich'.
The classic false friend: 'estar embarazada' = to be pregnant, not embarrassed ('avergonzado/a'). English 'embarrass' does come from the Spanish verb 'embarazar' (to hinder), via French.
From Latin 'civitas' (cf. 'city', 'civic'). Plural 'ciudades'. 'Ciudad de México' (CDMX) is the largest Spanish-speaking city. 'Ciudadano/a' = citizen.
From Latin 'populus'. A small town or village, and also 'the people' as a nation ('el pueblo español'). 'Mi pueblo' = my home town. English 'pueblo' is used for Native American villages.
'Ir al centro' = go into town, downtown. 'Centro de salud' = health centre; 'centro comercial' = mall. From Greek 'kentron' (sharp point).

From Latin 'platea' (cf. 'place', 'piazza'); borrowed by English as 'plaza'. Almost every Spanish town has a 'Plaza Mayor'. Also 'plaza de toros' (bullring) and 'plaza' = a job vacancy or parking space.
From Andalusi Arabic 'barri' (outside, suburb). Borrowed into English. 'Barrio Gótico' (Barcelona), 'La Boca' (Buenos Aires). 'De barrio' = local, neighbourhood (adj.).

The bench sense is Germanic (cf. 'bench'); the money sense came from Italian 'banco', because Renaissance bankers worked at benches. 'Banco de peces' = a shoal of fish. 'Bancarrota' = bankruptcy (broken bench).
From Latin 'ecclesia', from Greek 'ekklesia' (assembly; cf. 'ecclesiastical'). Capitalised for the institution ('la Iglesia católica'). Sunday mass is 'la misa'.
From Latin 'museum', Greek 'mouseion' (seat of the Muses). Madrid's 'Museo del Prado' and Bilbao's Guggenheim are the best known. Many are free on Sunday afternoons.
From French 'parc'. 'Parque de atracciones' = amusement park; 'parque nacional'; 'parque infantil' = playground. Madrid's 'El Retiro' is the famous one.
Short for 'cinematógrafo'. 'Ir al cine' = go to the movies; also film as an art ('el cine español'). Films are usually dubbed in Spain; 'V.O.' marks original-language showings.
From Greek 'theatron' (viewing place). 'Hacer teatro' = to put on an act, make a scene. Madrid's 'Teatro Real' is the opera house.
From Greek 'biblion' (book) + 'theke' (case). The false-friend pair: 'biblioteca' lends books, 'librería' sells them. 'Biblioteca Nacional de España' is in Madrid.
From 'ayuntar' (to join together, Latin 'adiunctare'): the council that meets. Both the building and the institution. Latin America says 'la municipalidad' or 'la alcaldía'.
From Latin 'aedificium' (cf. 'edifice', 'edify'). 'Edificio de oficinas' = office block. 'Edificar' = to build (formal).
Masculine, from Latin 'pons, pontis' (cf. 'pontoon'). 'Hacer puente' = to take a long weekend by 'bridging' a midweek holiday to the weekend, a beloved Spanish custom.
From Latin 'castellum'. The region of Castilla (Castile) is named after its many frontier castles. 'Castillos en el aire' = castles in the air.
Feminine. From Latin 'cathedra' (the bishop's chair); 'cátedra' is a university chair, 'catedrático' a full professor. Seville's is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world.
'La policía' is the force; an individual officer is 'el/la policía'. 'Poner una denuncia' = to report a crime at the 'comisaría'. Spain also has the 'Guardia Civil' outside cities.
'Pan' + the shop suffix '-ería', which names most shops: 'carnicería' (butcher's), 'frutería', 'pescadería', 'zapatería', 'papelería' (stationer's). 'Panadero/a' = baker.
From Greek 'stadion', originally a unit of length and the running track. The Santiago Bernabéu (Real Madrid) and Camp Nou (Barcelona) are the giants.
From Latin 'fons, fontis' (cf. 'font', 'fountain'). A fountain in a square, a natural spring, and a source of information. Also a serving dish. Madrid's 'Fuente de Cibeles' is a landmark.
From French 'pays'. The accent breaks the diphthong: pa-ÍS; plural 'países'. 'El País Vasco' = the Basque Country; 'El País' is Spain's main newspaper.
From 'peluca' (wig): originally a wig-maker's. 'Peluquero/a' = hairdresser; 'cortarse el pelo' = to get a haircut. A barber is 'el barbero'.
From Turkish 'köşk' (pavilion) via French 'kiosque'; also spelt 'kiosco'. The street stand that sells newspapers, magazines, sweets and lottery tickets.
The tables outside a bar or café: 'tomar algo en una terraza' is a Spanish ritual from spring to autumn. Also a rooftop terrace or a flat's balcony-terrace.
